Invisibility of God
in-viz-i-BIL-i-tee of GOD
noun phrase (theology proper / divine attributes)
The divine attribute by which God in His essence is invisible — not perceptible by physical sight. Grounded in 1 Timothy 1:17 (invisible), 1 Timothy 6:16 (whom no man hath seen, nor can see), John 1:18 (no man hath seen God at any time), and Colossians 1:15 (the invisible God). Closely related to the spirituality of God.

📖 Biblical Definition

The divine attribute by which God in His essence is invisible — not perceptible by physical sight. Closely related to the spirituality of God (because God is spirit, He is invisible). The biblical foundation: (1) 1 Timothy 1:17, the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God; (2) 1 Timothy 6:16, Whom no man hath seen, nor can see; (3) John 1:18, No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him; (4) Colossians 1:15, Christ is the image of the invisible God; (5) Exodus 33:20, the LORD's words to Moses, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live; (6) John 4:24 with John 6:46, Not that any man hath seen the Father, save he which is of God, he hath seen the Father. The doctrine holds that God in His essence cannot be seen by the physical eye; the theophanies of the OT (the visible manifestations of God — the burning bush, the glory-cloud, the appearances to the patriarchs) were accommodated visible manifestations of God's presence and glory, not the seeing of God's invisible essence; and the supreme revelation of the invisible God is the Lord Jesus Christ, who as the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15) and the only-begotten Son in the bosom of the Father has declared (made known) the invisible God (John 1:18). The eschatological hope includes the beatific vision — the seeing of God (Matthew 5:8, the pure in heart... shall see God; 1 John 3:2, we shall see him as he is; Revelation 22:4, they shall see his face) — understood by the Reformed tradition as the glorified saints' immediate and blessed knowledge-and-sight of God in a manner exceeding present comprehension, supremely in the face of Christ. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's invisibility against the idolatrous image-making (the attempt to make visible the invisible God), and grounds in it the central role of the Word (the invisible God reveals Himself by His Word, heard rather than seen) and the supreme revelation of God in Christ (the image of the invisible God who declares the Father).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The divine attribute by which God in His essence is invisible, not perceptible by physical sight; 1 Timothy 1:17 (invisible), 1 Timothy 6:16 (whom no man hath seen, nor can see), John 1:18, Colossians 1:15; supremely revealed in Christ the image of the invisible God; the eschatological beatific vision.

INVISIBILITY OF GOD, n. phr. (theology proper / divine attributes) God in His essence is invisible, not perceptible by physical sight; closely related to the spirituality of God. Foundation: 1 Timothy 1:17 (invisible); 1 Timothy 6:16 (whom no man hath seen, nor can see); John 1:18 (no man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son... he hath declared him); Colossians 1:15 (the invisible God); Exodus 33:20 (there shall no man see me, and live). The OT theophanies were accommodated manifestations of God's presence and glory, not the seeing of His essence. Supreme revelation of the invisible God: Christ, the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). The eschatological beatific vision (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Timothy 6:16 — "Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen."

John 1:18 — "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him."

Colossians 1:15 — "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature."

1 John 3:2 — "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The invisibility of God is held against idolatrous image-making (the attempt to make visible the invisible God); the invisible God reveals Himself by His Word and supremely in Christ the image of the invisible God.

expand to see more

The invisibility of God is held principally against idolatrous image-making. Because God in His essence is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17; 6:16; John 1:18), every attempt to make a visible image of God falsifies His invisible nature and constitutes idolatry (the second-commandment ground). The doctrine grounds the central role of the Word in true religion: the invisible God reveals Himself primarily by His Word, which is heard rather than seen; faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and the invisible God is known through His revealed Word, not through visible images. The supreme revelation of the invisible God is the Lord Jesus Christ: the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), the only-begotten Son who has declared (made known) the invisible Father (John 1:18); in Christ, the invisible God has made Himself known, not by an image we construct but by the Son He has sent. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: God in His essence is invisible; the OT theophanies were accommodated manifestations of His presence and glory, not the seeing of His essence; the invisible God is revealed by His Word and supremely in Christ; and the eschatological hope is the beatific vision — the glorified saints' blessed sight-and-knowledge of God, supremely in the face of Christ (1 John 3:2, we shall see him as he is; Revelation 22:4). The believer worships the invisible God through the Word and in Christ, refusing the idolatrous image-making that would make visible the invisible God, and awaits the beatific vision when faith shall give way to sight.

1 Timothy 1:17; 6:16; John 1:18; Colossians 1:15; Exodus 33:20; God invisible in essence; revealed by His Word and supremely in Christ; the eschatological beatific vision (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4).
